lead: For an input that is not changing, a sensor is fully described by a small set of numbers. Each number answers a different question: how close to truth (accuracy), how repeatable (precision), how small a change it can see (resolution), how much output per input (sensitivity), how straight its graph is (linearity), and how it behaves going up versus down (hysteresis) or over time (drift). These are the numbers on a datasheet, a calibration certificate and a purchase order. They let you compare a cheap pressure module with an expensive transmitter honestly.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for sensor types and Chapter 1.3 for the calibration line and units.

sections.h3: Range, span, sensitivity, accuracy and precision

blocks.text: Range is the two limits the sensor is made for, such as 0–250 kPa or −40 to 125 °C. Span is the difference between those limits: 250 kPa in the first example. A sensor can have a non-zero lower limit, for example 50–250 kPa, so range and span are not the same. Sensitivity is the slope of the output-versus-input graph:

blocks.where: S is sensitivity in output units per input unit (mV/kPa, mV/V per kPa, or counts/°C); Δy is a small output change; Δx is the input change that caused it.

blocks.text: For a straight sensor, S = output span / input span. A 0–50 mV output over 0–250 kPa gives S = 50 mV / 250 kPa = 0.2 mV/kPa.

Accuracy is how close the mean indicated value is to the true value. Quote it as ± value, ± % of full scale (%FS) or ± % of reading, and say which. Error is e = indicated − true. The fixed part of error is bias; the scatter of repeated readings is precision or repeatability, usually a standard deviation or a band.

Resolution is the smallest input change that gives a detectable output change. A display showing 100.1 kPa has resolution 0.1 kPa. Threshold is the smallest input that causes any output from rest. Dead band is an input range over which the output does not change. Resolution belongs to the whole chain: sensor, amplifier and display.

Linearity is the maximum deviation of the measured curve from a chosen straight line, as ± %FS. Three lines are named. Terminal-based (end-point) joins the two ends of the calibration curve. Best-fit (least-squares) minimises the sum of squared deviations. Independent picks the line with the smallest maximum deviation. Always name the line when quoting linearity.

blocks.where: L is linearity in %FS; y_meas is the measured output; y_line is the chosen straight-line output at the same input; y_span is the full-scale output span.

blocks.text: Hysteresis is the maximum difference between up-scale and down-scale readings at the same input, expressed as %FS. Friction, backlash or magnetic memory cause it. Drift is a slow change with time (zero drift, span drift) or temperature (thermal drift), quoted per month or per °C. Tolerance is the allowed manufacturing deviation from nominal. Also, ±1 %FS on a 0–250 kPa device is ±2.5 kPa at every reading; ±1 % of reading at 10 kPa is only ±0.1 kPa. At low readings, %FS is the larger number. Time-varying behaviour is Chapter 1.5.

sections.h3: A practical order for reading a datasheet

items: Fix range and span. Check that the working input sits inside the range with margin.
Find sensitivity and output span. Check the amplifier or ADC can accept that output.
Read accuracy with its reference: ± value, ± %FS or ± %reading.
Separate bias from precision. Calibration shows bias; repeated readings show scatter.
Compare resolution with the smallest change you must detect. A fine display does not fix a coarse sensor.
Check linearity and name the straight line used. Then check hysteresis and drift.
If low readings matter, convert %FS to the actual input at that reading.

blocks.text: The figure uses the same 0–250 kPa, 0.2 mV/kPa sensor. The ideal line is 0 mV at 0 kPa and 50 mV at 250 kPa. The measured curve has a small zero offset and a bow, so near mid-span it can sit about 0.6 mV above the line. At 0.2 mV/kPa that is 3 kPa. Statistical combination of these errors belongs to Chapter 1.6.

figure.caption: The ideal 0.2 mV/kPa line and the measured curve. Notice the small zero offset and the 0.6 mV bow near mid-span, equal to 3 kPa.

spec.aria: Output against pressure: the straight ideal line of slope 0.2 mV/kPa and the measured curve that sits 0.02 mV above zero and bows up to 0.6 mV away from the line near mid-span.

examples.question: A 0–250 kPa pressure sensor has output 0–50 mV. Ten repeated readings at a true pressure of 100 kPa have mean 99.6 kPa and sample standard deviation 0.5 kPa. The display resolution is 0.1 kPa. A calibration curve deviates from its straight line by at most 0.6 mV. Find sensitivity, bias error in kPa and %FS, precision band at 3σ in kPa and %FS, resolution in %FS, and linearity in kPa and %FS. Comment on accuracy, precision and linearity.
steps: Input span = 250 kPa; output span = 50 mV. S = 50 mV / 250 kPa = 0.2 mV/kPa.
Linearity in input = 0.6 mV / 0.2 mV/kPa = 3 kPa. As %FS: 3 / 250 × 100 = 1.2 %FS.
Reading: the mean is close to true (small bias), the scatter of 0.5 kPa is good precision, and linearity at 1.2 %FS is mediocre compared with the resolution.
examples.answer: S = 0.2 mV/kPa; bias = −0.4 kPa = −0.16 %FS; precision band = ±1.5 kPa = ±0.6 %FS; resolution = 0.1 kPa = 0.04 %FS; linearity = 3 kPa = 1.2 %FS; precision is good, bias is small, linearity is mediocre.
examples.check:
FS = 250.0
out_span = 50.0
true = 100.0
mean = 99.6
s = 0.5
res = 0.1
lin_mV = 0.6
S = out_span / FS
bias = mean - true
bias_pct = bias / FS * 100
prec = 3 * s
prec_pct = prec / FS * 100
res_pct = res / FS * 100
lin_kPa = lin_mV / S
lin_pct = lin_kPa / FS * 100
print(round(S, 10))
print(round(bias, 10))
print(round(bias_pct, 10))
print(round(prec, 10))
print(round(prec_pct, 10))
print(round(res, 10))
print(round(res_pct, 10))
print(round(lin_kPa, 10))
print(round(lin_pct, 10))

traps: Accuracy and precision are different. A sensor can be precise and still inaccurate by a fixed bias.
± %FS and ± %reading differ hugely at low readings. 1 %FS on 0–250 kPa is ±2.5 kPa anywhere; 1 % of a 10 kPa reading is only ±0.1 kPa.
Resolution is not sensitivity. High sensitivity with poor resolution is possible.
Linearity without naming the straight line is incomplete. Terminal-based, best-fit and independent linearity give different numbers.
Hysteresis is up/down at the same input; drift is change with time or temperature. A zero shift after warming is drift, not hysteresis.

quiz.q: Define range and span for a 0–250 kPa sensor.
quiz.a: Range is 0–250 kPa; span is 250 kPa.

quiz.q: What is the unit of sensitivity for a voltage-output pressure sensor?
quiz.a: mV/kPa, or mV per kPa; if ratiometric, mV/V per kPa.

quiz.q: Why can a sensor be precise but inaccurate?
quiz.a: Precision is scatter of repeated readings; accuracy is distance of their mean from true. A fixed bias shifts the mean while repeats stay close, so readings are precise but wrong by that bias.

quiz.q: A 0–200 kPa sensor gives 0–40 mV. Find sensitivity.
A 0–250 kPa sensor is quoted ±0.5 %FS. What error does that allow at 20 kPa? Compare with ±0.5 % of reading.
quiz.a: ±0.5 %FS = 0.005 × 250 = ±1.25 kPa at any input. ±0.5 % of 20 kPa = ±0.1 kPa. The %FS figure is much larger at this low reading.

quiz.q: A datasheet gives linearity 0.5 %FS and resolution 0.02 %FS. Which limits a static measurement more, and why?
quiz.a: Linearity limits it more: 0.5 %FS is 25 times 0.02 %FS. Resolution is fine, but the calibration curve can deviate by 0.5 %FS, so that deviation dominates the static error budget.

quiz.q: Distinguish threshold, dead band and resolution.
quiz.a: Threshold is the smallest input that gives any output from rest. Dead band is an input range with no output change. Resolution is the smallest input change that gives a detectable output change anywhere in range.

quiz.q: A sensor has hysteresis 0.3 %FS on a 0–250 kPa range. What is the maximum difference between up-scale and down-scale readings at the same input?
quiz.a: 0.3 %FS = 0.003 × 250 = 0.75 kPa. The up-scale and down-scale readings at the same input can differ by up to 0.75 kPa.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these static numbers become the accuracy budget in a calibration certificate, and %FS versus %reading decides whether a cheap 250 kPa transmitter is useless for a 10 kPa leak test. Smart sensors store their own calibration coefficients, so linearity and drift are corrected in firmware. Search for 'sensor accuracy specification %FS vs %reading', 'terminal-based linearity' and 'best-fit straight line calibration'. Unit 5, Smart sensors, and Unit 6, signal conditioning linearisation, build on this.
